title: Reflection starts with interception
question: Can the incident ray reach a receding mirror?
recap: First check that the light can catch the mirror: its speed along the mirror’s normal, c cos φ, must exceed the mirror’s speed away from it. Then change to the mirror’s rest frame, reflect the light there, and change back.
premises: The mirror is flat and perfectly reflecting, and it moves slower than light.
The light must be able to reach the mirror: c cos φ is greater than v.
limitations: Where the light only just fails to catch the mirror, a number from the calculation is not a reflection.
A reflected ray can still move towards +x in the laboratory, and a mirror receding faster moves away from it.

overview.text: First check that the light can catch the mirror: its speed along the mirror’s normal, \(c\cos\varphi\), must exceed the mirror’s speed away from it. Then change to the mirror’s rest frame, reflect the light there, and change back.

full.spoken: The reflected frequency ratio is one minus twice v over c cosine phi plus v over c squared, divided by one minus v over c squared.

full.text: At normal incidence and \(v = 0.6c\), three different ratios appear. The reflected light has one quarter of the incident frequency. The mirror intercepts incident energy at 0.4 times the rate of a fixed mirror, because it is moving away from the light. And with incident energy density \(u\), the light presses on the mirror with pressure \(0.5u\).

To count the energy the mirror intercepts, the moving-mirror laboratory uses the speed at which light crosses the moving surface, \(c\cos\varphi - v\), and not \(c\) alone. Light travelling parallel to the mirror in the original frame, with the mirror receding along positive \(x\), never reaches it, and the laboratory reports that no reflection happens.

full.returnCaption: Return to whether the light can reach a receding mirror.

steps.text:
Letters: the paper's mirror is the plane ξ = 0 of k, moving at v along x; the incident light has amplitude A, direction cosine cos φ and frequency ν in K, and the reflected light \(A'''\), \(\varphi'''\) and \(
u'''\); P is the light pressure and V the speed of light. \(
u_{\mathrm{ref}}\) below is the paper's \(
u'''\).

items: First, does the light reach the mirror? The light's speed along the mirror's normal is c cos φ, and the mirror recedes at v. If \(c\cos\varphi\) is not greater than v, the light never catches the mirror and there is no reflection to calculate.
Otherwise go to the mirror's frame k with §7's rules: \(A'=A\,q\), \(\cos\varphi'=(\cos\varphi-v/V)/(1-(v/V)\cos\varphi)\), \(\nu'=\nu\,q\), with \(q=(1-(v/V)\cos\varphi)/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\).
Reflect in k, where the mirror is at rest: \(A''=A'\), \(\cos\varphi''=-\cos\varphi'\), \(\nu''=\nu'\).

Transform back to K, with −v: each quantity gains the factor \((1+(v/V)\cos\varphi'')/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\). Put in \(\cos\varphi''\) and collect: \(A'''=A\frac{1-2\frac{v}{V}\cos\varphi+(v/V)^2}{1-(v/V)^2}\), as the paper prints it, and the frequency changes by the same factor.

steps.spoken: The reflected frequency ratio is one minus twice v over c cosine phi plus v over c squared, divided by one minus v over c squared.

items: Worked at normal incidence, v = 0.6c: \((1-1.2+0.36)/(1-0.36)=0.16/0.64\) = 0.25. The reflected light has a quarter of the incident frequency.

Energy arriving at unit area of the mirror per unit time, measured in K: \(\frac{A^2}{8\pi}(V\cos\varphi-v)\). The mirror recedes, so it intercepts light at the rate \(V\cos\varphi-v\), not V. At normal incidence and 0.6c that is 0.4 of a fixed mirror's rate.

Energy leaving unit area per unit time: \(\frac{A'''^2}{8\pi}(-V\cos\varphi'''+v)\). By the energy principle, the difference is the work the light pressure does per unit time, which the paper sets equal to P times v.
Solving gives the pressure, as printed: \(P=2\frac{A^2}{8\pi}\frac{(\cos\varphi-v/V)^2}{1-(v/V)^2}\).
Worked at normal incidence and 0.6c, with u the incident energy density \(A^2/8\pi\): \(P=2u\times0.16/0.64\) = 0.5 u.
To first order in v/V the paper recovers \(P=2\frac{A^2}{8\pi}\cos^2\varphi\), in agreement with experience and with other theories.

The paper's method in one line: transform the light to a frame in which the body is at rest, solve the problem of optics there, and transform back. It says every problem of the optics of moving bodies can be reduced this way to problems of the optics of bodies at rest.
The mirror here is ideal: its motion is prescribed, and it has no recoil, absorption or thickness.

steps.returnCaption: Return to whether the light can reach a receding mirror.

margin.text: The mirror here is ideal: its motion is prescribed, and it has no recoil, absorption or thickness. Einstein states the pressure in his Gaussian units; the SI form used here changes the units and leaves the result the same.
